extracted.intended_audience: aspiring orators, writers, and students of rhetoric/classical style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing sublime, elevated prose and oratory: when and how to use figures, images, diction, and structural devices to create grandeur, energy, and passion in literary and rhetorical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of sublimity (high-strung vs diffusive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between the sudden, vehement sublimity of Demosthenes and the diffused, widespread sublimity of Cicero/Plato.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use high-strung, abrupt, rapid, vigorous language when you want to exaggerate, rouse vehement emotion, or carry the audience with you; use the diffusive/extended style when you wish to overpower with a flood of language—suitable for familiar topics, perorations, digressions, descriptive/declamatory passages, history, natural science, and similar cases. (Metaphors: Demosthenes = whirlwind/thunderbolt; Cicero = widespread conflagration.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity arises from three sources
rubrics_metrics.description: On sublimity of thought, and the manner in which it arises from native greatness of mind, from imitation, and from the employment of images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate your own greatness of mind, emulate great predecessors, and employ potent images to develop sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emulation of great writers as a path to sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitate the great poets and prose-writers of the past (Homer, Plato, Demosthenes, Thucydides) to gather the divine impulse from another's spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix rivalry on high examples to guide and elevate your style; imitation is likened to copying from fair forms—useful and not plagiarism. Imagine how these masters would judge your work to incentivize exertion and refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagine exalted or future audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how Homer, Demosthenes, or future ages will listen to and judge your writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagining such judges or posterity will motivate higher care; but beware if this makes you unintelligible to contemporaries—balance timelessness with clarity for present readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of images (definition and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: An image includes every thought presented in speech; poets' images astound, orators' images give perspicuity; both work on emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oratorical images should have energy and reality and be mingled with practical argument so they enthrall as well as convince; avoid poetical/fabulous impossibilities in oratory which become offensive or monstrous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Images should be vivid and joined to argument
rubrics_metrics.description: An image adds energy and passion and, when mingled with practical parts of an oration, not only convinces but enthralls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place images within the argument to dominate weaker logical points and affect the audience emotionally (examples: Demosthenes' alarm/crime imagery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures of speech are essential to sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures, judiciously employed, play an important part in producing sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover only the most effective figures for grandeur; judicious, not indiscriminate, use is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophe / adjuration (use of oath)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of adjuration (apostrophe) to invoke ancestors/deities or to swearing by past heroes as a rhetorical device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ only in the right place, manner, occasion, and with the right motive; can exalt audience sentiment, heal a 'mind diseased', and confer grandeur—measure language so opponents have no handle (e.g., avoid words like 'conquered' if they invite rebuttal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical questions and self-interrogation
rubrics_metrics.description: The figures of question and interrogation stir an audience and give energy; self-questioning and answering reproduces meeting objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate question and answer quickly to simulate spontaneous passion and to blind judgment into perceiving inspiration rather than artifice; use where it seems to flow naturally from the occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid figures that breed suspicion unless cloaked
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures tend to rouse suspicion of dishonesty or false reasoning, especially before judges or rulers; a listener may feel treated like a 'silly boy' and react negatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To allay distrust, call in sublimity and passion: the brilliancy of sublime language can hide the artifices of figures; use grandeur to overshadow sophistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asyndeton (removal of connecting particles) for rush and urgency
rubrics_metrics.description: Omitting conjunctions/connecting particles gives a quick rush and 'torrent rapture' to a passage (e.g., 'they pushed, they fought, they slew, they fell').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to convey halted-and-hurried speech or intense agitation; creates vivid immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is so conducive to energy as combining two or three figures which mutually contribute to vigour, cogency, and beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unite devices (repetition, broken clauses, asyndeton, hyperbaton, etc.) to amplify force; examples: Demosthenes' repetition and broken sentences to imitate action and outrage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and broken clauses to imitate agitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeating words and breaking up sentences in lively descriptive passages imitates agitation and keeps passion moving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary movement constantly; irregularity can acquire a certain order and preserve intrinsic force; but follow with precise timing so effect is not merely disorderly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid smoothing passion with excessive conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding conjunctions and making logical sequence (Isocrates' style) will smooth away rapidity and rugged abruptness, diminishing the fire of passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid binding energetic passages into neat logical lists when immediacy and passion are required; use conjunctions when you desire calm order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbaton (transposition) to imitate violent agitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposition of words or thoughts from their usual order expresses violent mental agitation and gives an air of unpremeditated debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hyperbaton to imitate natural emotional dislocation (fear, rage, jealousy), to leave thoughts in suspense then return unexpectedly, and to drag the audience into the hazard; Thucydides and Demosthenes use it boldly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtaposition, enumeration, contrast, and climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting different cases side by side, enumerating particulars, and using contrast and climax add vigour, elevation, and life to style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ changes of case, time, person, number, and gender to add movement and diversity to diction; use in accordance with theme and permitted amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of plurals for singulars to magnify effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Plurals used for singulars or plural accumulation can give an impression of multiplied calamity or pomp (e.g., 'A countless host', 'There came forth Hectors').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when theme permits amplification or exaggeration; avoid overuse which becomes pedantic ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraction of plurals into singulars for corporate dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining many particulars into one singular (e.g., 'all Peloponnesus was divided' instead of 'all the cities') gives a sense of corporate life and dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ this knitting-together device to confer grandeur where combining particulars into a single sonorous subject enhances emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize past events by presenting them as present
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing past events as happening in present time changes narrative into dramatic action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the dramatic present to put the reader in the scene and make events immediate and vivid (examples from Xenophon, Thucydides).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interchange and direct address of persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Switching persons (second/first/third) or directly addressing the reader places them amid the perils described and excites interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct personal address and changes of person draw the reader into the scene, fix attention, and make them partakers in the action; use when you want immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sudden shift from third to first person as outburst
rubrics_metrics.description: A sudden step aside in narrative from third to first person strikes like an outburst of passion and creates immediate force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this device in urgent crises where preface would have a frigid effect; avoid interposing formal tags like 'he said' which damp the impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periphrasis for dignity and mellowness
rubrics_metrics.description: Periphrasis (roundabout expression) often lends harmony and dignity, investing simple words with melody and wider range of sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use periphrasis to harmonize and elevate thought (e.g., 'destined journey' for death) but ensure it is not inflated or harsh; balance with literal expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint with periphrasis (avoid abuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Periphrasis is liable to abuse: it can become feeble, vapid, and disgusting if overused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise great restraint; do not inflate trifling subjects with grand language; excessive ornament is pedantic and weakens effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of striking and appropriate words
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of appropriate and striking words has marvellous power—the main object of orators and writers; beautiful words are the 'light of thought.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select words that give grandeur, beauty, mellowness, dignity, energy, and power to thought; but avoid imposing lofty diction on trivial matters (don't put a huge tragic mask on a child).
